title: The Transfiguration (6 August)
hook: the light on the mountain in high summer
carry: it is good to be here

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joachim and Anne, Hannah's name among them, the grandparents the Bible never names. Your line was the old carry the faith. What did an older person tell you? Day six hundred seventy-eight.

Some evenings in August the light does something strange. The sun drops low, the air goes gold, and an ordinary street, a parking lot, a friend's face across a table, suddenly looks lit from inside. It's the kind of moment people try to photograph. Then it's gone, and it's just dusk. In the first week of August the Church remembers a moment like that, on a mountain, when three fishermen saw their teacher's face shine like the sun. And one of them, not knowing what to say, said something anyway.
screen: `AUGUST LIGHT.` → `LIT FROM INSIDE.` → `THREE FISHERMEN ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell it. Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, apart. And there he's transfigured before them: his face shines like the sun, his clothes turn dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appear, often read as the Law and the Prophets, talking with him. Luke adds what they talked about: his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. Then Peter, who never could stay quiet, says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles." Three tents. Let's stay. Mark adds, gently, that he didn't know what to say, because they were terrified. Then a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says: this is my beloved Son, hear ye him. When they look up, there's only Jesus. And they go back down the mountain. That's the shape of it. A moment of glory, and nobody gets to build a house there. The Gospels set it just after Jesus first tells them he will suffer and die, and some readers have heard it as a gift for the hard road ahead: a glimpse to remember on Good Friday. The Gospels never name the mountain. Tradition says Mount Tabor in Galilee, and a church stands there now. The feast is very old in the East, and in 1457 Pope Callixtus III extended it to the whole Western Church, on the sixth of August. The Greek verb Matthew uses is the root of our word metamorphosis.
screen: `HIS FACE SHONE LIKE THE SUN.` · `MOSES AND ELIJAH.` · `LET US MAKE THREE TENTS.` · `BACK DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.` · then, large: `LORD, IT IS GOOD FOR US TO BE HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the light change. If you can, go to a window or outside, ideally near sunset or sunrise, but any time will do. Pick one patch of sky, or one wall the light falls on, and just watch it. Notice the color shift, a cloud moving, a brightness fading or growing. Don't photograph it. Don't try to keep it. If you pray, you can say Peter's line once: it is good to be here. The bell holds the time.
The Transfiguration. Jesus shining on the mountain before Peter, James and John, with Moses and Elijah beside him. Its feast is the sixth of August. Today's word.
Your line: it is good to be here. Today, when something ordinary suddenly looks lit up, stop for one breath and say it. Then keep walking. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Transfiguration on 6 August, hearing one of the Gospel accounts of Jesus shining on the mountain; the same Gospel is also read on the Second Sunday of Lent.

what a scholar hears: Matthew's metamorphōthē; the mountain is unnamed in the Gospels; Callixtus III extended the feast in 1457.
